claim: Mutations in the synaptic gene SHANK3 lead to a neurodevelopmental disorder known as Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS).
source: Mutations in the synaptic gene SHANK3 lead to a neurodevelopmental disorder known as Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and background.

claim: PMS is a relatively common monogenic and highly penetrant cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID).
source: PMS is a relatively common monogenic and highly penetrant cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID), and frequently presents with attention deficits.
evidence: This statement is supported by epidemiological data cited in the manuscript.

claim: PMS frequently presents with attention deficits.
source: PMS is a relatively common monogenic and highly penetrant cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID), and frequently presents with attention deficits.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by the literature.

claim: The underlying neurobiology of PMS is not fully known.
source: The underlying neurobiology of PMS is not fully known and pharmacological treatments for core symptoms do not exist.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Pharmacological treatments for core symptoms of PMS do not exist.
source: The underlying neurobiology of PMS is not fully known and pharmacological treatments for core symptoms do not exist.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of therapeutic options.

claim: A Shank3-deficient rat model of PMS was produced with a genetic alteration similar to a human SHANK3 mutation.
source: Here, we report the production and characterization of a Shank3-deficient rat model of PMS, with a genetic alteration similar to a human SHANK3 mutation.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the methods and Figure 1.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats exhibit impaired long-term social recognition memory.
source: We show that Shank3-deficient rats exhibit impaired long-term social recognition memory and attention, and reduced synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex pathway.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats exhibit impaired attention.
source: We show that Shank3-deficient rats exhibit impaired long-term social recognition memory and attention, and reduced synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex pathway.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the 5-CSRT task presented in Figure 3.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats exhibit reduced synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex pathway.
source: We show that Shank3-deficient rats exhibit impaired long-term social recognition memory and attention, and reduced synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex pathway.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The deficits in Shank3-deficient rats were attenuated with oxytocin treatment.
source: These deficits were attenuated with oxytocin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The effect of oxytocin on reversing non-social attention deficits is a particularly novel finding.
source: The effect of oxytocin on reversing non-social attention deficits is a particularly novel finding, and the results implicate an oxytocinergic contribution in this genetically defined subtype of ASD and ID, suggesting an individualized therapeutic approach for PMS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The results implicate an oxytocinergic contribution in this genetically defined subtype of ASD and ID.
source: The effect of oxytocin on reversing non-social attention deficits is a particularly novel finding, and the results implicate an oxytocinergic contribution in this genetically defined subtype of ASD and ID, suggesting an individualized therapeutic approach for PMS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the oxytocin treatment results.

claim: The results suggest an individualized therapeutic approach for PMS.
source: The effect of oxytocin on reversing non-social attention deficits is a particularly novel finding, and the results implicate an oxytocinergic contribution in this genetically defined subtype of ASD and ID, suggesting an individualized therapeutic approach for PMS.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: More than 80% of individuals with PMS meet ASD diagnostic criteria.
source: It has been estimated that more than 80% of individuals with PMS meet ASD diagnostic criteria and that ~0.5–1% of ASD cases, 1–2% of ID cases, and up to 2% of cases with both ASD and ID harbor a SHANK3 mutation, which makes it one of the more common single locus causes of ASD and ID (Gong et al., 2012; Soorya et al., 2013; Leblond et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Approximately 0.5–1% of ASD cases harbor a SHANK3 mutation.
source: It has been estimated that more than 80% of individuals with PMS meet ASD diagnostic criteria and that ~0.5–1% of ASD cases, 1–2% of ID cases, and up to 2% of cases with both ASD and ID harbor a SHANK3 mutation, which makes it one of the more common single locus causes of ASD and ID (Gong et al., 2012; Soorya et al., 2013; Leblond et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Approximately 1–2% of ID cases harbor a SHANK3 mutation.
source: It has been estimated that more than 80% of individuals with PMS meet ASD diagnostic criteria and that ~0.5–1% of ASD cases, 1–2% of ID cases, and up to 2% of cases with both ASD and ID harbor a SHANK3 mutation, which makes it one of the more common single locus causes of ASD and ID (Gong et al., 2012; Soorya et al., 2013; Leblond et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Up to 2% of cases with both ASD and ID harbor a SHANK3 mutation.
source: It has been estimated that more than 80% of individuals with PMS meet ASD diagnostic criteria and that ~0.5–1% of ASD cases, 1–2% of ID cases, and up to 2% of cases with both ASD and ID harbor a SHANK3 mutation, which makes it one of the more common single locus causes of ASD and ID (Gong et al., 2012; Soorya et al., 2013; Leblond et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SHANK3 mutations make PMS one of the more common single locus causes of ASD and ID.
source: It has been estimated that more than 80% of individuals with PMS meet ASD diagnostic criteria and that ~0.5–1% of ASD cases, 1–2% of ID cases, and up to 2% of cases with both ASD and ID harbor a SHANK3 mutation, which makes it one of the more common single locus causes of ASD and ID (Gong et al., 2012; Soorya et al., 2013; Leblond et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited epidemiological data.

claim: No pharmaceutical compounds targeting core symptoms of PMS are available.
source: To date, no pharmaceutical compounds targeting core symptoms of PMS are available.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of therapeutic options.

claim: Several mouse lines with distinct Shank3 gene mutations have been developed.
source: To address this lack of effective therapeutics, several mouse lines with distinct Shank3 gene mutations have been developed to help understand the neurobiology of the syndrome and as a means of ultimately developing and assessing potential therapeutics (Bozdagi et al., 2010; Peça et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012; Kouser et al., 2013; Kloth et al., 2015; Bidinosti et al., 2016; Mei et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Shank3-deficient mouse models have displayed PMS and ASD-related behavioral phenotypes including impaired social behavior, increased repetitive behaviors, and motor deficits.
source: The various Shank3-deficient mouse models have displayed PMS and ASD-related behavioral phenotypes including impaired social behavior, increased repetitive behaviors, and motor deficits, as well as altered synaptic transmission and neuronal morphology in the brain (Bozdagi et al., 2010; Peça et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012; Kouser et al., 2013; Drapeau et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Shank3-deficient mouse models have displayed altered synaptic transmission and neuronal morphology in the brain.
source: The various Shank3-deficient mouse models have displayed PMS and ASD-related behavioral phenotypes including impaired social behavior, increased repetitive behaviors, and motor deficits, as well as altered synaptic transmission and neuronal morphology in the brain (Bozdagi et al., 2010; Peça et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012; Kouser et al., 2013; Drapeau et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IGF-1 improves motor and synaptic deficits observed in a Shank3-deficient mouse line.
source: Recently, the translational relevance of these mouse models has been highlighted by our observation that the hormone IGF-1 improves motor and synaptic deficits observed in a Shank3-deficient mouse line (Bozdagi et al., 2013), a result which directly led to a safety and preliminary efficacy clinical trial of IGF-1 in children with PMS (Kolevzon, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The observation that IGF-1 improves deficits in Shank3-deficient mice directly led to a safety and preliminary efficacy clinical trial of IGF-1 in children with PMS.
source: Recently, the translational relevance of these mouse models has been highlighted by our observation that the hormone IGF-1 improves motor and synaptic deficits observed in a Shank3-deficient mouse line (Bozdagi et al., 2013), a result which directly led to a safety and preliminary efficacy clinical trial of IGF-1 in children with PMS (Kolevzon, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Founder Shank3-deficient rats were generated using zinc-finger nucleases (ZFN) technology, targeting exon 6 of the ankyrin repeat domain.
source: Founder Shank3-deficient rats were generated using zinc-finger nucleases (ZFN) technology, targeting exon 6 of the ankyrin repeat domain.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used to generate the rat model.

claim: Five patients had been described with mutations in the ankyrin repeat domain of SHANK3.
source: This domain was targeted because five patients had been described with mutations in it (Figure 1A) (Durand et al., 2007; Moessner et al., 2007; Hamdan et al., 2011; Boccuto et al., 2013; Yuen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and Figure 1A.

claim: The predicted truncated protein generated upon ZFN targeting of the rat Shank3 gene is quite similar to one of the human mutations that have been described.
source: Interestingly, the predicted truncated protein generated upon ZFN targeting of the rat Shank3 gene is quite similar to one of the human mutations that have been described (Hamdan et al., 2011) (Figure 1A, middle sequence).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a cited human mutation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mutation in the rat Shank3 gene leads to a significant reduction in the number of Shank3 transcripts.
source: In rat, this mutation leads to a significant reduction in the number of Shank3 transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and reduces expression levels of the full-length Shank3a protein (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mutation in the rat Shank3 gene reduces expression levels of the full-length Shank3a protein.
source: In rat, this mutation leads to a significant reduction in the number of Shank3 transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and reduces expression levels of the full-length Shank3a protein (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The levels of the PSD scaffolding protein Homer1 are decreased in the Shank3-deficient rats.
source: We also observed that the levels of the PSD scaffolding protein Homer1 are decreased in the Shank3-deficient rats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), consistent with changes in the PSD and with well-replicated findings from Shank3-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The decrease in Homer1 levels in Shank3-deficient rats is consistent with changes in the PSD and with well-replicated findings from Shank3-deficient mice.
source: We also observed that the levels of the PSD scaffolding protein Homer1 are decreased in the Shank3-deficient rats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), consistent with changes in the PSD and with well-replicated findings from Shank3-deficient mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to previous findings in mice.

claim: At weaning, there was a modest reduction in the number of homozygous knockout (KO) animals from Heterozygous (Het) x Het matings, compared to expectation.
source: We noted that, at weaning, there was a modest reduction in the number of homozygous knockout (KO) animals from Heterozygous (Het) x Het matings, compared to expectation (292:555:200, corresponding to ratios of 0.53:1:0.36).
evidence: This is based on observed breeding ratios.

claim: No genotype-related deficits were found in basic developmental or functional processes in Shank3-deficient rats.
source: We found no genotype-related deficits in these basic developmental or functional processes.
evidence: This is based on developmental assessments described in the methods.

claim: Shank3-Het and KO rats did not exhibit increased anxiety-like behaviors when tested on the elevated plus maze.
source: In addition, when tested on the elevated plus maze, Shank3-Het and KO rats did not exhibit increased anxiety-like behaviors (See Materials and methods for details and Supplementary file 1 for results).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data.

claim: No differences were found between Shank3-deficient and wildtype (WT) rats in preference for a social stimulus versus an object.
source: We first measured preference for a social stimulus versus an object (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), as well as juvenile social play (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and adult dyadic social interactions (Supplementary file 1) in freely interacting animals. We found no differences between Shank3-deficient and wildtype (WT) rats in any of these measures of social behavior or social preference.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No differences were found between Shank3-deficient and wildtype (WT) rats in juvenile social play.
source: We first measured preference for a social stimulus versus an object (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), as well as juvenile social play (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and adult dyadic social interactions (Supplementary file 1) in freely interacting animals. We found no differences between Shank3-deficient and wildtype (WT) rats in any of these measures of social behavior or social preference.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No differences were found between Shank3-deficient and wildtype (WT) rats in adult dyadic social interactions.
source: We first measured preference for a social stimulus versus an object (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), as well as juvenile social play (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and adult dyadic social interactions (Supplementary file 1) in freely interacting animals. We found no differences between Shank3-deficient and wildtype (WT) rats in any of these measures of social behavior or social preference.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data.

claim: Shank3-deficiency does not impair short-term social recognition memory.
source: We found that Shank3-deficiency does not impair short-term SRM as shown by the comparable findings between WT and Shank3-deficient rats on the social habituation-dishabituation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and short-term SD tests (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Shank3-Het and KO rats were unable to discriminate between novel and familiar social stimuli in the long-term social discrimination test.
source: In contrast, in two independent cohorts, we found that Shank3-Het and KO rats were unable to discriminate between novel and familiar social stimuli in the long-term SD test (Figure 2B) as they spent equal time investigating both the familiar and novel social stimuli.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Total investigation time (toward both familiar and unfamiliar rats) did not differ across genotypes in any of the social discrimination tests.
source: Notably, total investigation time (toward both familiar and unfamiliar rats) did not differ across genotypes in any of the SD tests (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating there is not a decreased interest in social exploration.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The fact that Shank3-Het and KO rats performed well on the short-term SD test ruled out perceptual deficits.
source: Moreover, the fact that the Shank3-Het and KO rats performed well on the short-term SD test and were able to perceive and remember their conspecifics, even when only given 5 min for the first interaction, also ruled out perceptual deficits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data.

claim: Shank3-Het and KO rats performed similarly to their WT littermates in the object location memory test.
source: In contrast to the impaired behavior in the long-term SD test, Shank3-Het and KO rats performed similarly to their WT littermates in the object location memory and contextual fear conditioning memory tests (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Shank3-Het and KO rats performed similarly to their WT littermates in the contextual fear conditioning memory test.
source: In contrast to the impaired behavior in the long-term SD test, Shank3-Het and KO rats performed similarly to their WT littermates in the object location memory and contextual fear conditioning memory tests (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Shank3 deficiency selectively impairs long-term social memory, but leaves intact both short-term social memory and non-social long-term memory.
source: These results indicate that Shank3 deficiency selectively impairs long-term social memory, but leaves intact both short-term social memory and non-social long-term memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: Attention deficits are often associated with PMS.
source: Attention deficits are often associated with PMS.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMS.

claim: Shank3-Het and KO rats learned the 5-CSRT task and were able to reach baseline, similar to WT controls.
source: Shank3-Het and KO rats learned the task and were able to reach baseline, similar to WT controls.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data.

claim: Shank3-Het and KO rats had lower accuracy and lower omission rates in the 5-CSRT task, when compared to WT rats, even after extensive training.
source: However, both the Shank3 Het and KO rats had lower accuracy and lower omission rates, when compared to WT rats, even after extensive training.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3.

claim: After reaching baseline criterion, Shank3-deficient rats did not maintain even this level of performance across the 10-day test period.
source: Moreover, after reaching baseline criterion Shank3-deficient rats did not maintain even this level of performance across the 10-day test period, during which they performed significantly fewer correct trials (Figure 3A), made more errors (Figure 3B), and exhibited higher omission rates than WT rats (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats performed significantly fewer correct trials than WT rats during the 10-day test period of the 5-CSRT task.
source: Moreover, after reaching baseline criterion Shank3-deficient rats did not maintain even this level of performance across the 10-day test period, during which they performed significantly fewer correct trials (Figure 3A), made more errors (Figure 3B), and exhibited higher omission rates than WT rats (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats made more errors than WT rats during the 10-day test period of the 5-CSRT task.
source: Moreover, after reaching baseline criterion Shank3-deficient rats did not maintain even this level of performance across the 10-day test period, during which they performed significantly fewer correct trials (Figure 3A), made more errors (Figure 3B), and exhibited higher omission rates than WT rats (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats exhibited higher omission rates than WT rats during the 10-day test period of the 5-CSRT task.
source: Moreover, after reaching baseline criterion Shank3-deficient rats did not maintain even this level of performance across the 10-day test period, during which they performed significantly fewer correct trials (Figure 3A), made more errors (Figure 3B), and exhibited higher omission rates than WT rats (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: On trials with a correct response, Shank3-deficient rats responded more slowly and with more variable latencies than WT rats.
source: Even on trials with a correct response, Shank3-deficient rats responded more slowly and with more variable latencies than WT rats (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Slow, inaccurate and omitted responses to very brief visual stimuli are commonly interpreted as reflecting an attention deficit.
source: Slow, inaccurate and omitted responses to very brief visual stimuli are commonly interpreted as reflecting an attention deficit (Robbins, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Sensory perception deficits were excluded as an explanation for the 5-CSRT task deficits in Shank3-deficient rats.
source: While changes in accuracy might also be attributed to deficits in sensory perception, we excluded this possibility by carrying out studies with less bright visual cues and Shank3-deficient rats performed at WT levels (not shown).
evidence: This is based on additional behavioral testing.

claim: The 5-CSRT task deficits in Shank3-deficient rats were only manifested when the duration of the light cues was shortened, which indicates impaired vigilance and/or spatial attention.
source: It was only when the duration of the light cues was shortened that the deficits were manifested, which indicates impaired vigilance and/or spatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: The 5-CSRT task deficits in Shank3-deficient rats were not due to decreased motivation for food.
source: Furthermore, these deficits were not due to decreased motivation for food, because the latency of Shank3-deficient rats to collect reward after a correct response was similar to WT rats (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), as was task performance when light cues were of a longer duration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Shank3-deficient rats are impaired in an attentionally demanding task.
source: In summary, these results indicate that Shank3-deficient rats are impaired in an attentionally demanding task, which, when considered together with the deficits in long-term social memory, indicates this model demonstrates face validity for some features of PMS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 5-CSRT task results.

claim: The Shank3-deficient rat model demonstrates face validity for some features of PMS.
source: In summary, these results indicate that Shank3-deficient rats are impaired in an attentionally demanding task, which, when considered together with the deficits in long-term social memory, indicates this model demonstrates face validity for some features of PMS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results.

claim: Memory deficits have been associated with ASD.
source: Memory deficits, while not considered core symptoms of autism, have been associated with ASD (Boucher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Impaired working memory has been observed in human subjects with ASD.
source: Both impaired working (Barendse et al., 2013) and episodic memory (Maister et al., 2013) have been observed in human subjects with ASD, which has been attributed to aberrant connectivity of the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Ben Shalom, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Impaired episodic memory has been observed in human subjects with ASD.
source: Both impaired working (Barendse et al., 2013) and episodic memory (Maister et al., 2013) have been observed in human subjects with ASD, which has been attributed to aberrant connectivity of the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Ben Shalom, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Memory deficits in ASD have been attributed to aberrant connectivity of the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: Both impaired working (Barendse et al., 2013) and episodic memory (Maister et al., 2013) have been observed in human subjects with ASD, which has been attributed to aberrant connectivity of the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Ben Shalom, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The behavioral deficits observed in Shank3-deficient rats are consistent with dysfunction in hippocampal and mPFC circuits.
source: The behavioral deficits we observe in Shank3-deficient rats are consistent with dysfunction in these circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results and known circuit functions.

claim: The hippocampus and mPFC are both important for social recognition memory.
source: The hippocampus and mPFC are both important for SRM (Watson et al., 2012; Harvey and Lepage, 2014; Jacobs and Tsien, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Performance in the 5-CSRT task depends on mPFC function.
source: Moreover, performance in the 5-CSRT task depends on mPFC function (Rogers et al., 2001) and attention, working memory, and decision-making require intact hippocampal-prefrontal functional connectivity (Jones and Wilson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Attention, working memory, and decision-making require intact hippocampal-prefrontal functional connectivity.
source: Moreover, performance in the 5-CSRT task depends on mPFC function (Rogers et al., 2001) and attention, working memory, and decision-making require intact hippocampal-prefrontal functional connectivity (Jones and Wilson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Extracellular field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fESPs) recordings at Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses were similar between genotypes.
source: Extracellular field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fESPs) recordings at Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses were similar between genotypes, with no differences in paired-pulse facilitation (Supplementary file 1) or the input-output relationship (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no differences in paired-pulse facilitation at Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses between genotypes.
source: Extracellular field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fESPs) recordings at Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses were similar between genotypes, with no differences in paired-pulse facilitation (Supplementary file 1) or the input-output relationship (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: Basal synaptic transmission is generally intact in Shank3-deficient rats.
source: These results suggest that basal synaptic transmission is generally intact in Shank3-deficient rats.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) induced by high-frequency stimulation (HFS) was reduced in both Shank3-Het and KO rats at Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses.
source: We found, however, in independent cohorts, that plasticity at these synapses was not intact. Long-term potentiation (LTP) induced by high-frequency stimulation (HFS) was reduced in both Shank3-Het and KO rats (Figures 4A and 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while mGluR-dependent long-term depression (LTD) was reduced only in KO rats (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figures 4A, 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mGluR-dependent long-term depression (LTD) was reduced only in KO rats at Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses.
source: We found, however, in independent cohorts, that plasticity at these synapses was not intact. Long-term potentiation (LTP) induced by high-frequency stimulation (HFS) was reduced in both Shank3-Het and KO rats (Figures 4A and 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while mGluR-dependent long-term depression (LTD) was reduced only in KO rats (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Innervation of the mPFC by the hippocampus is important for attention and working memory.
source: Innervation of the mPFC by the hippocampus (Marquis et al., 2006) is important for attention and working memory, both of which we have shown here are impaired in Shank3-deficient rats.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LTP was reduced in both Shank3-Het and KO rats in the hippocampal-PFC synaptic pathway in vivo.
source: We therefore assessed hippocampal-PFC synaptic transmission in vivo by stimulating hippocampal CA1/subicular regions and recording fEPSPs in the prelimbic area of the PFC in anesthetized rats. We found that LTP was reduced in both Shank3-Het and KO rats (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were no genotype associated differences in the input-output relationship of evoked local field potentials in coronal PFC slices.
source: We also observed that there were no genotype associated differences in the input-output relationship of evoked local field potentials in coronal PFC slices, which demonstrates that these changes were specific to hippocampal-prefrontal circuitry (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: The changes in synaptic plasticity were specific to hippocampal-prefrontal circuitry.
source: We also observed that there were no genotype associated differences in the input-output relationship of evoked local field potentials in coronal PFC slices, which demonstrates that these changes were specific to hippocampal-prefrontal circuitry (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: Shank3-deficiency impairs plasticity in both the projections from hippocampus to the PFC and within intrinsic hippocampal circuits.
source: In summary, these results suggest that Shank3-deficiency impairs plasticity in both the projections from hippocampus to the PFC and within intrinsic hippocampal circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: Oxytocin has a central role in social recognition memory formation.
source: Oxytocin has a central role in SRM formation (Ferguson et al., 2000; Gur et al., 2014) and hence we reasoned that it may underly some of the altered behaviors we observed; in addition and more broadly, oxytocin modulates mammalian social behavior and may be dysregulated in ASD (Harony and Wagner, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oxytocin modulates mammalian social behavior and may be dysregulated in ASD.
source: Oxytocin has a central role in SRM formation (Ferguson et al., 2000; Gur et al., 2014) and hence we reasoned that it may underly some of the altered behaviors we observed; in addition and more broadly, oxytocin modulates mammalian social behavior and may be dysregulated in ASD (Harony and Wagner, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Oxytocin improved the long-term social memory deficits in Shank3-Het and KO rats.
source: We observed that oxytocin improved both the long-term social memory and attention deficits in Shank3-Het and KO rats (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Oxytocin improved the attention deficits in Shank3-Het and KO rats.
source: We observed that oxytocin improved both the long-term social memory and attention deficits in Shank3-Het and KO rats (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In WT animals, oxytocin had no effect on long-term social recognition memory.
source: Notably, in WT animals, oxytocin had no effect on long-term SRM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or 5-CSRT task performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In WT animals, oxytocin had no effect on 5-CSRT task performance.
source: Notably, in WT animals, oxytocin had no effect on long-term SRM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or 5-CSRT task performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Oxytocin has been previously shown to enhance the induction of synaptic plasticity in several systems.
source: Since oxytocin reversed the behavioral deficits in Shank3-deficient rats and has been previously shown to enhance the induction of synaptic plasticity in several systems (Benelli et al., 1995; Tomizawa et al., 2003; Fang et al., 2008; Ninan, 2011; Lin et al., 2012; Gur et al., 2014), we also examined the effect of oxytocin on LTP both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In acute hippocampal slices derived from WT rats, oxytocin enhanced LTP induction after a weak stimulation of one train of 100 Hz pulses.

evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and supported by citations.

claim: Oxytocin-dependent enhancement of LTP after weak stimulation was not observed in Shank3-deficient rats.

claim: In WT slices, oxytocin had no effect on LTP induced by stronger stimulation (4 × 100 Hz stimulation trains).

evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Oxytocin greatly enhanced LTP induced by stronger stimulation in slices prepared from Shank3-deficient rats.

evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In vivo, oxytocin reversed the impaired LTP at hippocampal-prefrontal synapses in Shank3-deficient rats.
